sections.overview: The San Marcos salamander is a tiny, permanently aquatic plethodontid endemic to the headwaters of the San Marcos River in Texas.
sections.identification: Adults are dark reddish brown and slender, about 2.5–5 cm long, with large eyes and prominent external gills retained throughout life.
sections.habitat: It lives in clear, flowing spring water among gravel, rocks, moss and algae; muddy or bare bottoms are unsuitable.
sections.diet: It eats small aquatic crustaceans, insects and snails; federal sources also list midge larvae and aquatic insect nymphs.
sections.behavior: It remains aquatic and often waits among submerged vegetation or algae for prey; the dark back blends with the algal habitat.
sections.reproduction: Texas Parks and Wildlife reports eggs laid singly or in small groups on plants or beneath rocks. FWS notes that wild courtship and egg laying have not been observed.
sections.ecology: The nearby Barton Springs Salamander, Eurycea sosorum, is a different species: genetic studies assign salamanders at northern Hays County springs to E. sosorum, not E. nana; see its profile.
sections.conservation: It has been federally and state-listed as threatened since 1980; declining spring flow, groundwater pollution and siltation threaten its restricted habitat.
